# OIDC Sign-In Implementation

## Status: spec draft (no product code)

## Completed

- Draft spec: `design.md` (43 acceptance criteria), `decisions.md` (ADR-001 to ADR-009), `customer-questions.md`, `breakdown.md`.
- Code reading on `origin/main` at `e01d161c0c` (facts in design.md, Technical Design).

## In Progress

- Team review of the breakdown and owners.
- Customer questions not yet posted on #131.

## Blocked

- Sub-issue 7 (account linking) waits on customer Q1 and Q8.
- Sub-issue 1 waits on a yes for the `schema.prisma` change.
- Sub-issue 9's password-login switch waits on customer Q4.

## Sprint 3 slice (demo by 2026-11-19)

Path: an admin adds one Keycloak provider in **Settings → Admin → Identity providers** (secret encrypted), the login page shows "Continue with <name>", a user with a verified email signs in against the local Keycloak and gets a new Cal.diy account, and a user with an unverified email sees the `unverified-email` message. A first login whose email matches an existing account is rejected with `oidc-account-exists`; that is the safe rule under every answer to Q1, so the slice does not wait on the customer.

Sub-issues on the path and merge order:

1. Sub-issue 1 (data model and repository). Everything else needs it.
2. Sub-issue 3 (admin service and tRPC) and sub-issue 5 (per-request providers and new-user sign-in), in parallel.
3. Sub-issue 4 (admin page, after 3) and sub-issue 6 (login buttons and errors, after 5).
4. Sub-issue 2 (Keycloak) at any time; the demo needs it.

Demo script: start Keycloak; sign in as the instance admin; add the provider; Test connection; enable; sign out; click the button; sign in as the verified Keycloak user (new account, onboarding); sign out; sign in as the unverified user (error page).

Moves to Sprint 4: sub-issues 7, 8, 9 (linking, settings page, removal with counts, password-login switch, Playwright test).

Risk: sub-issue 5 is the largest and touches the 1,255-line `next-auth-options.ts`. Start it on day one after sub-issue 1 merges. Keep the change to that file to two delegation calls (top of `signIn`, top of `jwt`) and the `getOptions` argument.

## Next Steps

1. Team agrees on the breakdown and fills owners.
2. Zachary posts the breakdown and the questions on #131 (after the team agrees).
3. Create sub-issues 1–9 with one assignee each; add 1–6 to the Sprint 3 milestone.
4. Owner of sub-issue 1 asks for the schema yes, then writes the full sub-issue spec.
5. Each owner gets a spec-review comment before code.

## Session Notes

- 2026-11-09: Spec drafted from #131 and code reading. `login-view.tsx` does not read `?error=` from the URL, so next-auth's `OAuthSignin` / `OAuthCallback` redirects show nothing today; criterion 22 and sub-issue 6 cover it. The `signIn` branch at L1012 lets any verified non-`CAL` login enter an existing non-`CAL` account by email; a naive `OIDC` enum value would fall into it (criterion 28).

# OIDC Sign-In Future Work

Ideas and enhancements deferred from the initial implementation.

## Enhancements

- Map provider groups or claims to Cal.diy roles and teams (customer Q9).
- Single logout at the provider (out of scope in #131).
- Per-provider button icon and color.
- API v2 endpoints for provider management.
- Show the last sign-in error and time for each provider on the admin page.

## Technical Debt

- If the per-request provider query shows in profiles, add a cache behind the repository with cross-instance invalidation (ADR-001, option 2).
- The secret uses AES-256-CBC without authentication, like other stored credentials. Moving all of them to an authenticated mode is a separate change.

## Nice to Have

- A mock OIDC server for CI, if Keycloak is too heavy for CI runs (ADR-008, option 3).

39:39:4. The issuer URL must be `https`. `http` is accepted only for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or a `*.localhost` host, so that a local test provider works. Scopes must include `openid`.
51:51:13. Clicking a button starts an authorization code flow with PKCE and `state` checks. User data comes from the ID token claims (`idToken: true`).
52:52:14. A first login with a verified email, no existing Cal.diy user with that email, "allow new accounts" on, and the email domain on the allowed list (or no list): Cal.diy creates a user with `identityProvider = OIDC`, `emailVerified` set, the name from the `name` claim, and an `Account` row for (provider id, `sub`). The user lands in onboarding.
53:53:15. A login where `email_verified` is missing or `false` is rejected with `/auth/error?error=unverified-email` and the existing message `unverified_email_oauth_error`. No user and no `Account` row is created or changed.
54:54:16. A login with no `email` claim is rejected with a new error `missing-email` and a message that tells the user to ask their admin to release the email claim. Nothing is created.
55:55:17. A login with no `name` claim does not fail. The name falls back to `preferred_username`, then to the part of the email before `@`. (Today `signIn` returns `false` for a missing name, at `next-auth-options.ts:847`.)
56:56:18. A first login when "allow new accounts" is off, or the email domain is not on the allowed list, is rejected with a new error `oidc-signup-not-allowed`. The message says the account does not exist and names no reason that would reveal the domain list.
57:57:19. A returning linked user signs in as the user that owns the `Account` row, found by (provider id, `sub`), never by email. This holds after the user's email changes at the provider.
58:58:20. A linked user with Cal.diy 2FA enabled still gets the TOTP step (`loginWithTotp`), as Google users do today.
59:59:21. A user who sends a forged or expired `state`, or replays a callback, gets the login page with a "sign-in failed, try again" message, and no session.
63:63:22. Provider down, slow (no answer in 5 seconds) or discovery URL unreachable when the user clicks the button: the user returns to the login page with the message "We could not reach <display name>. The login page must read and show `OAuthSignin`, `OAuthCallback` and `AccessDenied`.
64:64:23. Wrong client secret or wrong client ID: the token exchange fails, and the user sees "Sign-in with <display name> is not set up correctly. Contact your administrator." The server logs the provider id and the error code, not the secret.
65:65:24. A provider that is disabled or removed while a user is on its login page: the callback is rejected with the message from criterion 23. No user is created.

Exit code 1
## ADR-002: How a user's OIDC link is stored

Status: Proposed. Needs a yes before any edit to `schema.prisma`.

### Context

`User.identityProvider` is one enum (`CAL | GOOGLE | SAML | AZUREAD`) and `User.identityProviderId` is one string. Admins create providers at run time, and two providers can issue the same `sub`. `getIdentityProvider` returns `null` for unknown ids, which sends `signIn` to `unknown-provider` and `jwt` to the email-based auto-merge.

### Options Considered

1. **One `OIDC` enum value; the link is an `Account` row with `provider = "oidc-<id>"`, `providerAccountId = sub`.** Pros: `Account` already has `@@unique([provider, providerAccountId])`, so one `sub` per provider maps to one user; a user can hold links to several providers; no `User` column change. Cons: OIDC lookups must use `Account`, not `User.identityProviderId`, so the OIDC path cannot share the existing lookup at L891.
2. **One `OIDC` enum value plus a new `User.identityProviderConfigId` column.** Pros: keeps the existing `identityProvider + identityProviderId` lookup. Cons: one link per user only, so linking a second provider overwrites the first; a second migration on the largest table.
3. **One enum value per provider.** Cons: enums are fixed at migration time, so an admin cannot add one at run time. Rejected outright.

### Decision

Option 1. New OIDC users get `identityProvider = OIDC` and `identityProviderId = sub` for display only. Existing users who link a provider keep their `identityProvider`, so their password or Google login keeps working.

### Consequences

- `getIdentityProvider` maps the `oidc-` prefix to `OIDC`.
- Removing a provider means deleting its `Account` rows (criterion 37).
- `requiresTwoFactorSetup` treats `OIDC` as non-`CAL`, so OIDC users are exempt from site-wide 2FA unless the customer says otherwise (Q6).

## ADR-003: Provider id in URLs and `Account.provider`

Status: Proposed.

### Options Considered

1. **Immutable database id (`oidc-<cuid>`).** Pros: renaming the display name never breaks links or the registered callback URL. Cons: the callback URL is not human-readable.
2. **Admin-chosen slug (`oidc-university`).** Pros: readable URL. Cons: editing the slug breaks every link and the URL registered at the provider, so the slug would have to be locked after creation, which is option 1 with extra rules.

### Decision

Option 1.

## ADR-004: What happens when an OIDC email matches an existing account

Status: **Customer** (Q1). We propose; we do not pick. This path gets a narrow Deep (Fable 5.1) review before implementation.

### Context

Any provider an admin adds can assert any email, including the email of the instance admin. Google and Microsoft use `allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking: true` and the `signIn` branches at L1012 and L1051 merge on a verified email. If OIDC used the same paths, a misconfigured or hostile provider, or a user who can set their own email at a self-service provider, could take over any account. The `jwt` callback's `autoMergeIdentities()` (L453) also finds the user by `token.email`, so a wrong `true` from `signIn` becomes a session for the email's owner.

### Options Considered

1. **Auto-link on verified email.** Pros: no friction; matches Google and Microsoft today. Cons: account takeover whenever a provider asserts an email it does not own. Self-service providers (Keycloak with user registration on, or a provider that lets users edit their email) make this easy.
2. **Reject and require linking from settings.** The user signs in with their existing method, then clicks "Link" in Settings → Security, which proves control of both accounts. Pros: no takeover path; simple to test. Cons: one extra step for every existing user at roll-out.
3. **Auto-link only for allowed domains.** Each provider has a list of email domains the admin says the provider owns. A verified email in that list auto-links; any other match is rejected as in option 2. Accounts with role `ADMIN` never auto-link. Pros: smooth roll-out for the organization's own domain; takeover risk limited to domains the admin vouched for. Cons: more rules to test; a wrong list is still a takeover path for that domain.

### Proposal to the customer

Option 3 with option 2 as the fallback, and no auto-link for `ADMIN` accounts. Sprint 3 ships option 2 only (reject), because it is safe under every answer and the Sprint 3 demo needs only new accounts.

### Consequences

- The OIDC branch must never fall through to L1012, L1021, L1051 or `autoMergeIdentities()`. A test per branch (criterion 28).
- Linking from settings (sub-issue 6) is needed for existing users under options 2 and 3.

## ADR-005: Where the OIDC logic sits in `signIn` and `jwt`

Status: Proposed.

### Options Considered

1. **A separate OIDC branch at the top of `signIn`, in its own service (`OidcSignInService`), returning before the shared code.** Pros: the shared Google/Azure/SAML branches stay untouched (Google and Microsoft are out of scope); the OIDC rules are testable without the 400-line callback; follows the factory rule (conditionals at the entry point). Cons: some duplication of user-creation code.
2. **Add `OIDC` cases to the existing branches.** Pros: less new code. Cons: every existing branch gains an OIDC condition; a missed condition is a takeover (ADR-004); review must re-read all of `signIn`.

### Decision

Option 1. `signIn` checks `account.provider.startsWith("oidc-")` once and delegates. The `jwt` callback does the same and resolves the user from the `Account` row.

## ADR-006: How the client secret is stored

Status: Proposed.

### Options Considered

1. **Encrypt with `symmetricEncrypt` and `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in the provider row.** Pros: existing precedent (`packages/lib/crypto.ts`); no new dependency; works with criterion 1. Cons: anyone with the database and the key can read secrets; AES-256-CBC without authentication (same as existing credentials).
2. **Store the name of an environment variable that holds the secret.** Pros: secret never in the database. Cons: needs an environment change and restart for each new provider, which fails criterion 1.
3. **Store plain text.** Cons: a database dump leaks every secret. Rejected.

(Hashing is not possible: the server must send the secret to the provider.)

### Decision

Option 1. The secret is write-only in the UI and absent from every DTO.

## ADR-007: User data from the ID token or the userinfo endpoint

Status: Proposed.

`cd /Users/zachshort/Developer/csci-435-se/cal.diy/specs/oidc-sign-in && sed -n '120,160p' decisions.md; printf '\n#### design 130-160\n'; sed -n '130,160p' design.md`

```text
### Options Considered

1. **ID token claims (`idToken: true`).** Pros: signed by the provider and checked against its JWKS; one fewer request. Cons: some providers put `email` only in userinfo unless configured.
2. **Userinfo endpoint.** Pros: always has the profile claims. Cons: extra request that can fail; data not signed.

### Decision

Option 1. If the ID token has no `email`, the login fails with `missing-email` (criterion 16), and the admin docs say how to release the claim in Keycloak, Authentik and Okta.

## ADR-008: Test identity provider

Status: **Owner** (where the compose service lives).

### Options Considered

1. **Keycloak in a separate compose file under `specs/oidc-sign-in/test-idp/` (or `docker/`), with a realm export.** Pros: real provider; teammates who do not work on OIDC run nothing new; no change to the shared `docker-compose.yml`. Cons: one more command to start.
2. **Add Keycloak to `docker-compose.yml`.** Pros: one command. Cons: every teammate pulls and runs a ~500 MB image; changes a shared file.
3. **A small mock OIDC server (for example `oidc-provider` in Node) for unit and CI tests.** Pros: fast, scriptable claims. Cons: not a real provider; a new dev dependency (needs a yes).

### Proposal

Option 1 for manual and end-to-end tests; unit tests mock the provider response and need no server. Option 3 only if CI needs it later.

## ADR-009: Removing a provider that users depend on

Status: Proposed.

### Options Considered

1. **Allow delete with a typed confirmation that shows linked and only-login user counts; delete the `Account` rows; users recover by password reset.** Pros: admin stays in control; nobody loses data. Cons: some users must reset a password.
2. **Block delete while any user is linked; offer disable only.** Pros: no one loses a login. Cons: an admin who changed providers can never clean up.
3. **Delete with no warning.** Cons: silent lock-out. Rejected.

### Decision

Option 1, plus disable (criterion 38) as the reversible choice the page offers first.

#### design 130-160
### Database Changes (needs a yes before any edit to `schema.prisma`)

- Add `OIDC` to `enum IdentityProvider` (`schema.prisma:367`).
- Add model `OidcProvider`: `id` (cuid, immutable, used in the NextAuth provider id `oidc-<id>`), `displayName`, `issuer`, `clientId`, `clientSecretEncrypted`, `scopes`, `allowSignup` (default false), `allowedDomains` (String[]), `enabled` (default false), `position` (Int), `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `updatedById`.
- No change to `User` or `Account`. The link is an `Account` row with `provider = "oidc-<id>"` and `providerAccountId = sub`. `@@unique([provider, providerAccountId])` (L1258) already makes one `sub` belong to one user per provider. See ADR-002.

### Server

- `PrismaOidcProviderRepository` (data access only) and `OidcProviderService` (validation, encryption, discovery test), wired with the moduleLoader DI pattern in `packages/features/auth/oidc/di/`.
- `apps/web/pages/api/auth/[...nextauth].ts` becomes an async handler that loads enabled providers and passes them to `getOptions`. `getOptions` gains a `dynamicProviders` argument and stays synchronous. See ADR-001.
- Each provider becomes a NextAuth `type: "oauth"` provider with `wellKnown`, `idToken: true`, `checks: ["pkce", "state"]`, and **no** `allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking`. `httpOptions.timeout` is set to 5000 ms (to confirm the option name for next-auth 4.24.13).
- `getIdentityProvider` maps any id that starts with `oidc-` to `IdentityProvider.OIDC`. `signIn` gets a separate OIDC branch before the shared code, so OIDC never reaches the auto-merge branches (criterion 28). The `jwt` callback resolves OIDC users through the `Account` row, not through `token.email`.
- New-user and link paths call `calcomAdapter.linkAccount` inside `signIn`, so that next-auth's own callback handler finds the account by (provider, `sub`) and does not need email linking. (To confirm with a test: next-auth 4 runs `signIn` before its account lookup.)
- Admin tRPC procedures under `viewer.admin`: `oidcProviders.list`, `create`, `update`, `setEnabled`, `delete`, `testDiscovery`. All use `authedAdminProcedure`. List returns a DTO without the secret.
- Public read for the login and sign-up pages: id and display name of enabled providers only, read in `getServerSideProps`.

### UI

- Admin: new page `apps/web/app/(use-page-wrapper)/settings/(admin-layout)/admin/identity-providers/page.tsx` (role check here), view in `apps/web/modules/settings/admin/identity-providers-view.tsx`. Follows `security/page.tsx`.
- Login: buttons in `apps/web/modules/auth/login-view.tsx` after the Microsoft button (~L215), using `signIn("oidc-<id>")` and `useLastUsed`. Read `error` from the URL and show it.
- Error page: add messages for `missing-email`, `oidc-signup-not-allowed`, `oidc-account-exists`, `unknown-provider` in `apps/web/app/(use-page-wrapper)/auth/error/page.tsx`.
- Settings → Security: "Connected logins" section (Sprint 4).
- Every string goes in `packages/i18n/locales/en/common.json`. The existing `sso_oidc_*` strings belong to the removed team SSO feature; reuse `sso_oidc_callback_copied` only.

## Edge Cases

Covered by the criteria above. The short list:

- Provider down, slow, unreachable discovery, bad secret, issuer mismatch: 5, 22–26.
- Unverified, missing email, missing name: 15–17.
- Email matches an existing account, invited user, two providers with one email: 27–30.
```

If the OIDC branch, or `jwt`, reuses the lookups `where { identityProvider: idP, identityProviderId }` (NAO L891–911, L914–932, L601–612), a provider B (hostile, misconfigured, or one with user-chosen subs) asserting victim's sub at provider A matches the victim. In `jwt` L601→L758 the token's `id` is set from this lookup, ignoring the user next-auth already resolved by Account. L908 `mode: "insensitive"` makes it worse. Rule: for `oidc-*` the only identity lookup is `Account(provider, providerAccountId)`; `jwt` sets `id` from `user.id`; never query `identityProviderId` for OIDC (better: do not store `sub` there, or store `oidc-<id>:<sub>`). ````markdown
Hi @ojcchar, before we finish the spec for #131 we need your decision on the points below. For each one we give our proposal; please confirm it or tell us what you want instead. Q1 and Q2 block implementation.

**Blocking**

1. **Same email as an existing account.** Someone logs in with OIDC for the first time, and the provider says their verified email is `ana@uni.edu`. A Cal.diy account with `ana@uni.edu` already exists and is not linked to that provider. Any provider an admin adds can assert any email, so merging on email alone lets a misconfigured provider take over accounts. We propose:
   - (a) The admin lists the email domains each provider owns (for example `uni.edu`). A verified email in that list links to the existing account automatically.
   - (b) Any other match is rejected with a message telling the user to sign in their usual way and link the provider in Settings → Security.
   - (c) Accounts with the admin role never link automatically.

   Is this what you want? Or should every match be rejected (only (b)), or should every verified match link?
2. **Who may create a new account through OIDC?** We propose a per-provider switch "allow new accounts" (off by default) and an optional list of allowed email domains. Is that right? Should the existing instance setting that disables sign-up also block OIDC sign-up?

**Need an answer this sprint**

3. **Providers that do not send `email_verified`.** Some providers leave out this claim. We propose to reject those logins (the #131 criterion), with no admin option to treat emails as verified. Do you agree?
4. **Turning off password login.** Do you want a switch that disables password login when OIDC is set up? If yes, we propose that users with the admin role can always log in with a password, so no one can lock every admin out. We plan this for Sprint 4.
5. **Removing a provider.** When an admin removes a provider that users log in with, we propose: show how many users are linked and how many have no other login; require the admin to type the provider name; keep those users' accounts and data; and let them set a password with "Forgot password". Disabling a provider (hide it, keep links) is offered first. Is that right?
6. **Two-factor authentication.** The site-wide "require 2FA" setting (#112) applies only to password users today. Should OIDC users also be forced to set up Cal.diy 2FA, or does their identity provider's MFA count?
7. **Email changes at the provider.** A linked user's email changes at the provider. We propose to update the Cal.diy email at the next login if the new email is verified, not used by another account, and in the provider's allowed domains. Otherwise the login is rejected. Do you agree?
8. **Invited users.** An admin or team invited `bo@uni.edu`, who has not accepted yet. Should the first OIDC login with that email take over the invited account, or be treated like Q1?

**Can wait for Sprint 4**

9. **Groups to roles.** We propose that provider groups do not give Cal.diy roles in this feature (recorded as future work). Do you agree?
10. **Unlinking.** We propose that a user can unlink a provider in Settings → Security unless it is their only way to log in; then they must set a password first. Do you agree?
11. **Number of providers.** We propose up to 10 providers, shown on the login page in an order the admin sets. Is that enough?
12. **Test provider.** We will test against Keycloak running locally. Is Keycloak acceptable as the reference provider, or do you want us to test Authentik or Okta too?
13. **Upgrade.** After the upgrade, nothing changes until an admin adds a provider. Downgrading after providers exist is not supported. Is that acceptable?

Thanks!
````

# Claude in Chrome

Claude in Chrome is a browser extension. Its tools, named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`, act in the person's real Chrome, in new tabs alongside the person's own, with their existing sign-ins. Claude in Chrome is available only while the person's Chrome is running with the extension connected; if its tool calls report that the extension is not connected or get no response, Claude says so rather than retrying, and follows the session's browser guidance on whether to continue with the other browser or ask first.

If the only Claude in Chrome tool present is `enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome`, Claude calls it first: it turns Claude in Chrome on for this conversation, and the `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*` tools appear once it has run.

## Loading the tools

If the `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*` tools are deferred (meaning they have to be loaded through ToolSearch before use), Claude loads every tool it expects to need in ONE ToolSearch call, because the select query accepts a comma-separated list and each extra ToolSearch call costs a full round trip. The core set to start with:

```
ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"
```

Claude adds task-specific tools to that same call when the task obviously needs them: `read_console_messages` and `read_network_requests` for debugging, `form_input` for forms, `gif_creator` for recordings, `javascript_tool` for page scripting. A second ToolSearch is only for a tool the task turned out to need later.

## Starting a session: tab context first, then a new tab

At the start of each browser session Claude calls `mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp` first, to see the person's current tabs and understand what they may want to work with. Then:

1. Claude reuses an existing tab only when the person explicitly asks to work with it.
2. Otherwise Claude opens a new tab with `mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp` and works there, and, unless the person wants them kept, closes the tabs it created before finishing.
3. Claude never reuses tab IDs remembered from an earlier or different session. If a tool reports that a tab does not exist or is invalid, or the person closes a tab, or a navigation error occurs, Claude calls `tabs_context_mcp` again for fresh tab IDs.

## Site permissions

Claude in Chrome acts on a site only once the person has allowed it; depending on their settings the person may be prompted per site, in the extension or in the app. When a tool call is waiting on or refused that permission, Claude tells the person and waits for them to allow it rather than working around it. A site the person declines is their decision; Claude moves on.

## Recording a GIF

For multi-step interactions the person may want to review or share, Claude can record them with `mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator`. Claude captures a few extra frames before and after each action so playback is smooth, and gives the file a meaningful name (for example "login_process.gif").

## Reading console output

`mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages` reads the page's console. Console output can be verbose, so when Claude is looking for specific entries it passes the `pattern` parameter (a regular expression), for example pattern "[MyApp]" to keep only the application's own logs.

## Alerts and dialogs

Claude does not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or other browser modal dialogs through its actions. Those dialogs block all further browser events, so the extension stops receiving commands. Instead:

1. Claude avoids clicking elements likely to raise a confirmation dialog (for example a "Delete" button) unless necessary.
2. If it must interact with such an element, Claude warns the person first that this may interrupt the session.
3. Claude can use `mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool` to check for and dismiss an existing dialog before proceeding, and prefers `console.log` plus `read_console_messages` over `alert` for debugging.

If a dialog does get triggered and the browser stops responding, Claude tells the person they need to dismiss it manually in Chrome.

## Staying on task, and when to stop

Claude stays focused on the specific task and does not wander into unrelated pages. Claude stops and asks the person how to proceed, explaining what it tried and what went wrong, when any of these happen:

- browser tool calls fail or return errors after 2 or 3 attempts
- the extension gives no response
- page elements do not respond to clicks or input, or pages do not load or time out
- the task turns out to involve unexpected complexity or tangents
- several approaches have not completed the task

Claude does not keep retrying the same failing action.

@Zach Bowden had Claude AI review PR #125 and run the existing tests along with additional regression tests. All 45 existing tests passed, but Claude created temporary tests in a separate copy of the repository and reproduced a few potential issues:

Fully booked days showing a blank panel: Claude tested a date where every appointment slot was booked. Instead of displaying “All booked” and the option to join the waitlist for that date, the component rendered a blank panel. Claude traced this to AvailableTimes.tsx, where an empty slots array causes the component to return early.

Six-hour waitlist hold being shortened or deleted: Claude created a six-hour reservation hold using the waitlist repository, then simulated the existing booking flow. When the booking page reserved the slot, the hold was shortened to approximately five minutes. When the slot was released, the hold was deleted entirely.

Duplicate waitlist offers: Claude simulated a failure during hold creation followed by a background-task retry, as well as two tasks running simultaneously. In both scenarios, the tests showed that the same available slot could be offered to two different people.

Title: Sprint 3 - CSCI 435/535 — Software Engineering (William & Mary — Fall 2026)
URL: https://csci-435-se.github.io/sprint3/
Source element: <article>
---
Sprint 3: Project Development & Testing¶

Nov 3 – Nov 19 · All deliverables due Nov 19, 11:59 PM (mid-sprint check-in due Nov 12) · 100 points (12% of course grade)

Sprint 3 continues the development of your project and puts the focus on testing: how well your tests check what your code is supposed to do. The issue backlog, PR workflow, and general expectations carry forward; see Sprint 1 and Sprint 2 for anything not explicitly changed here. This page covers what is new or different in Sprint 3.

Sprint 3 at a glance

Key dates: Nov 12: check-in + at least one code PR (open or merged) · Nov 19: everything else

Important rules (they cost the most points):

No merge without an approval on the latest commit.
Spec review on the issue, saying what was checked.
Every code PR links its issue.
Real AI logs.
Test Evidence table in every PR; expected values not copied from the code's output.
Mutation testing with a tool, before and after reports committed.
Your team introduces no new test failures; skipped tests and disabled checks need an issue.

Unfamiliar with a term?

Check the Glossary for definitions of terms used throughout this page.

Before you begin¶
Check your AI log setup against the AI Log Instructions before your first session.
Read "Things that must improve" below. These issues were observed in Sprint 2 and will be graded strictly.
Record your baseline early (see D8): the test results at your Sprint 2 release tag (-csci435-s2), from CI or by running the relevant test suites locally. It helps you find hardening issues and get the mutation tool running.
Try the mutation testing tool early (see D6), on any existing file in the part of the code you work on. Do not wait until your PRs are ready.
What is new in Sprint 3¶
Mutation testing (D6): a new individual deliverable. It replaces the UML diagrams from Sprint 2.
Test evidence section in every PR description (D4).
Hardening issues: one of your issues may be a hardening issue (D1).
Suite health section in the sprint report (D8).
Mid-sprint check-in requires an open PR (D7), due Nov 12.

Team feature for Sprints 3–4

Each team will be assigned a larger feature that spans Sprints 3 and 4. The instructor or TA will post it as an issue in your team's issue tracker and notify your team when it is posted. You will likely need to split it into sub-issues.

Things that must improve from Sprint 2¶

These issues were observed in Sprint 2 and will be graded strictly in Sprint 3.

1. Open PRs early. In Sprint 2, most PRs were opened in the last two days, which left no time for review. In Sprint 3, you need a code PR by the mid-sprint check-in (see D7).

2. Independent approval before merging. A PR is merged only after a teammate approves its latest commit. Merging without an approval, or after pushing new commits since the approval, is not allowed. Once approved, the author may merge. To keep reviews moving, request the review on GitHub and notify your reviewer on Zulip; reviewers respond (approve or request changes) within 24 hours.

3. Spec reviews must be visible and show what was checked. Before coding starts, a teammate posts a review comment on the issue itself. The comment states what the reviewer checked: whether each acceptance criterion is clear and testable, which cases were considered (and whether they are covered), and whether the scope fits. If the reviewer finds problems, they list them and the author updates the spec. If the spec is good, the reviewer says so and approves, but "Looks good!" with nothing about what was checked is not acceptable.

4. Link PRs and issues. Every code PR must link the issue it addresses, so the PR can be checked against the spec. Use Closes #<issue> in the PR description so the issue closes automatically when the PR is merged, and attach issues and code PRs to the Sprint 3 milestone.

5. AI logs must be real logs. A log shows your prompts and the AI's output (SpecStory format recommended; see the AI Log Instructions). The following are not logs and receive no full credit: summaries of a session, paraphrased prompts, a share link to a chat, or tool output without the prompts that produced it. File names must follow YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md. Link the log from the issue or PR it documents.

6. The sprint report must render. Check that tables and links display correctly on GitHub (no escaped \| or \[). Use the Sprint 3 sections, not a copy of a previous report.

Deliverables¶
D1 - Sprint Backlog¶

Same process as Sprint 2 (D1), including the priority on carryovers: unfinished Sprint 2 issues go into your Sprint 3 backlog first, or you document on the issue why they are dropped.

Scope minimums for Sprint 3 (same as Sprint 2):

Role Minimum issues
Each CSCI 435 member at least 2 medium issues (or equivalent story points)
Each CSCI 535 (grad) member at least 2 medium issues + 1 additional small issue (or equivalent story points)

Scope must be justified. Each issue states its scope (small or medium) and one or two sentences on why: which components it touches and how much change you expect. The instructor or TA may reclassify an issue whose scope is clearly overstated.

Hardening issues (optional). One of your issues may be a hardening issue: work that makes the existing system more reliable rather than adding a feature. Good sources:

Your baseline run (see D8): failing tests, flaky tests, or broken CI checks on main.
Tech debt your team recorded in the "Introduced" and "Encountered" fields of your Sprint 1 and Sprint 2 PRs.
Known bugs found in reviews, after merging, or by teammates.
The upstream issue tracker, for bugs in the parts of the system your team works on.

A hardening issue is scoped like any other issue (see the scope justification above). It must also include evidence that the problem is fixed:

Bug fix: a test that fails before the fix and passes after.
Flaky test: the root cause, and enough repeated runs of that test before and after the fix to show the change (for example, 20 runs for a unit test or 10 for an E2E test).
Broken or missing CI check: links to CI runs before and after the fix.
Failing tests in the baseline: pass/fail counts before and after, and the cause of each group of failures.

Regenerating snapshots, reformatting code, or silencing a check without fixing its cause counts as small at most.

Team feature. When the team feature issue is posted (see the box under "What is new in Sprint 3"), split it into sub-issues, each with its own owner, spec (D2), and scope. Link each sub-issue to the feature issue. Sub-issues count toward your scope minimum like any other issue. When the feature is posted, add its sub-issues to your Sprint 3 milestone and adjust your backlog as needed.

Create a Sprint 3 milestone in GitHub and attach all selected issues to it.

What to provide in D8 (Sprint report): link to the Sprint 3 milestone and the rationale for your backlog decisions.

D2 - Requirements Specification¶

Same format and requirements as Sprint 1 (D2). Specs must be written and reviewed before coding begins; see item 3 in "Things that must improve" for what counts as a review.

Hardening issues use a bug format (include the observed and expected behaviors, the steps to reproduct the issue, and other details about the issue) when they fix a defect. Otherwise, use a short task format: the problem, the goal, acceptance criteria, and other necessary details.

D3 - Design Decisions¶

Same as Sprint 2 (D3): each decision names at least two concrete alternatives and explains the choice.

D4 - Code Changes and Pull Requests¶

Same workflow as Sprint 2 (D4), including the Tech Debt section. Sprint 3 adds a Test Evidence section to every PR description. It replaces the "how it was tested" part of the description, so you don't write it twice.

## Test Evidence

| Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
|---|---|---|---|
| AC1: ... | ... | ... | ... |

**Not tested automatically, and why:** [...]

**AI-written tests:** [Which tests were written or modified by AI, and how you
checked that their expected values are correct. If none, write "None."]

How to fill it in:

One row per acceptance criterion from D2. For bug reports, use the Expected Behavior instead. For PRs that change no product behavior (for example, CI changes), write "N/A" and explain why.
Test(s): the test name (and file, if not obvious). If you checked the AC manually, write Manual: followed by the steps and what you saw. If an AC is tested both automatically and manually, list both in the same row.
Level: unit, integration, E2E, or manual.
Source of expected value: where the expected result in your test comes from. Use one of: AC, issue discussion, docs, upstream behavior, or other (explain). The current output of your own code is not a valid source; a test whose expected value was copied from what the code returns cannot detect that the code is wrong.
Not tested automatically, and why: only for ACs checked manually only.
You may use AI to draft this section, but you are responsible for checking that it is accurate.

Example:

Acceptance criterion Test(s) Level Source of expected value
AC1: An end date before the start date is rejected with an error outOfOffice.schema.test.ts › rejects end before start unit AC
AC2: The away badge appears on the booking page during the out-of-office window booking-ooo.e2e.ts › shows away badge in window E2E AC
AC3: The badge text is readable in dark mode Manual: enabled dark mode, opened the booking page during the window → badge text is readable manual issue discussion

Not tested automatically, and why: AC3 depends on visual contrast, which our test setup does not check.

If your fork has no CI that runs your tests, include in the PR description the command(s) you ran and a summary of the results (passed, failed, skipped).

Reviewers add one line to the code review rubric (Sprint 1, D4):

Criterion Score (1–10) Notes
Test evidence — does every AC have a test? Are the expected values justified? Which tests did you run locally?
D5 - AI Logs¶

Same requirements as Sprint 1 (D5) and the AI Log Instructions, with the enforcement described in item 5 of "Things that must improve."

Log storage: ai-logs/sprint3/<your-github-username>/

D6 - Mutation Testing (new)¶

This is a new individual deliverable.

What it is. A mutation testing tool makes small changes to your code (mutants), such as flipping a condition or changing a boundary value, and runs your tests against each one. If a test fails, the mutant is killed. If all tests pass, the mutant survived: your tests did not notice that the code changed. Survivors point to weak or missing tests.

What to do. For one of your issues whose PR changes source code and tests (CSCI 535: two such issues; your small issue may be one of them):

Run a mutation testing tool on the source files changed by your PR(s) for that issue. Do not run it on the whole project.
Using the tool's report, analyze every surviving mutant: is it equivalent (it behaves exactly like the original code, so no test can kill it), or does it reveal a gap in your tests? If there are more than 10 surviving mutants, analyze at least 10, starting with those in lines your PR added or changed.
Add or strengthen at least one test that kills a surviving mutant that revealed a gap. Re-run the tool to confirm it is killed. If no surviving mutant reveals a gap (all are killed or equivalent), say so and justify it in the surviving-mutants table; that completes this step.
Answer the questions in the template below.

Evidence. Configure the tool to write a machine-readable report (StrykerJS: add "json" to reporters; Gremlins: --output=<file>.json; go-mutesting: save the terminal output to a text file). Commit the report from your first run and from your re-run as docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/<issue#>-<username>-before.json and -after.json (.txt for go-mutesting). The mutation scores you list must match the reports, and the mutant your new test kills must show as killed in the "after" report.

A tool is required. Manual mutation does not count.

Stack Tool
TypeScript/JavaScript with Vitest (Actual Budget, Cal.diy, Excalidraw, Outline, Gitea frontend) StrykerJS with the Vitest runner
TypeScript/JavaScript with Jest (Medusa) StrykerJS with the Jest runner
Go (Gitea backend) Gremlins or go-mutesting

Set it up early. Getting the tool to work on a large codebase is real work: builds, services, and choosing which tests run. Each student configures and runs the tool for their own files and commits the configuration they used. You may reuse a teammate's setup (and are encouraged to), as long as you run the tool yourself and credit the teammate in your report.

Common problems to watch for:

The tool stops before mutating. Tools first run your tests on the unchanged code. If any of the selected tests fail, the run stops. Fix or exclude failing tests first (this is where your baseline run helps).
Tests run against built code. If your tests run against compiled output (for example, a dist folder) instead of the source, mutants in the source are never seen by the tests. Configure the tool to rebuild before testing, or choose tests that run on source.
Tests need services. Some test suites need a database or another service running. Start them before running the tool.
False survivors. If you limit which tests run (for example, with Vitest's dir option), make sure the tests that cover the mutated files are included. Otherwise, mutants that some test would catch are reported as survived or not covered. Before writing a new test for a survivor, check that the relevant tests actually ran.
Long runs. Mutating only the files changed by your PR keeps run time manageable.

If you are blocked

If you cannot get the tool to run, first ask your teammates: someone may already have a working setup. If you are still stuck, tell the TA as early as possible, with the errors you got and the AI log of what you tried. The TA will help you debug it. If it still cannot be made to work, the TA may approve running the tool on a different issue or a different part of your code instead. Problems reported at the end of the sprint will not excuse a missing D6.

Submission: docs/sprint3/mutation/<issue#>-<username>.md, using this template:

# Mutation testing: Issue #<N> -- <issue title>

**PR(s):** #... **Tool:** ... **Config:** [link; credit the teammate if you reused their setup] **Command:** `...`
**Reports:** [before](reports/<issue#>-<username>-before.json) · [after](reports/<issue#>-<username>-after.json)
**Mutation score:** before ...% → after ...%

## Surviving mutants

| Location (file:line) | Mutation | Equivalent or test gap? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |

## New or strengthened test

Commit: [link] · Test: [file › test name] · Kills: [mutant location]

## Questions

1. What did the surviving mutants reveal about your tests?
2. Did any surviving mutant point to an assertion whose expected value was not based on the requirements? Explain.
3. If you used AI to configure the tool, analyze survivors, or write tests, what did it produce and what did you verify or correct? If AI was not used, write "N/A."

D7 - Mid-Sprint Check-in¶

Due: Nov 12, 11:59 PM.

Submission: docs/sprint3/checkin/<username>.md

Format: ~100 words per question, plus a link.

What have you implemented so far, and what remains?
What is one thing you learned about testing in your project?
What is one risk to finishing your work by Nov 19, and what will you do about it?

Required link: at least one code PR you authored, open and ready for review, or merged, by Nov 12.

D8 - Sprint Report¶

Same format as Sprint 1 (D6 in Sprint 1), with these additions:

Suite health (new section). Keep it short:
Baseline table for the test suites relevant to your team (the packages or areas you work on, not the whole repository). For each suite: the command or CI workflow, and the test runner's summary line (passed, failed, skipped) at your Sprint 2 release tag (-csci435-s2) and at the end of the sprint. Use CI results where available; if you run tests locally, run only the packages you change.
Failures grouped by cause (for example: environment-specific, already broken upstream, flaky, caused by our changes), with a link to one issue per cause that lists the affected tests.
No failures introduced by your team. Any test your team's changes broke must be fixed by the end of the sprint. Pre-existing failures only need to be recorded and grouped; fixing them is optional (and can be a hardening issue).
Skipped tests and disabled CI checks. Skipping a test or disabling a CI check requires a linked issue and a reason in a code comment.
Mutation testing: links to each member's D6 file.
Hardening issues: which issues they are and where they came from.
Carryovers from Sprint 2 and what changed.

Submit to: docs/sprint3/report.md (or .pdf, .docx). If you submit Markdown, check that it renders on GitHub.

D9 - Sprint Release¶

Same as Sprint 1 (D7 in Sprint 1). Tag with the -csci435-s3 suffix.

Create the release after the last Sprint 3 merge, so it matches the final state of main. The release description summarizes the sprint's changes (features, fixes, hardening work), not just the tag name.

D10 - Reflection Survey (Individual)¶

Each team member must complete the Sprint 3 reflection survey individually. The link will be distributed via Blackboard and Zulip toward the end of the sprint.

Deadline: Nov 19, 11:59 PM.

Grading¶

Sprint 3 is worth 100 points (12% of the course grade). D1, D8, and D9 are graded as a team; all other deliverables are graded individually.

Deliverable Points Notes
D1 - Sprint Backlog 10 Team. Issues selected, scoped with justification, assigned, milestone created; carryover decisions documented
D2 - Requirements Specification 20 Individual. User story format, INVEST criteria, acceptance criteria quality; spec review on the issue before coding, showing what was checked
D3 - Design Decisions 5 Individual. At least one non-trivial decision per issue, with alternatives
D4 - Pull Requests 20 Individual. See detail below
D5 - AI Logs 5 Individual. Real logs, correctly named, linked from the issue or PR
D6 - Mutation Testing 15 Individual. See rubric below
D7 - Mid-Sprint Check-in 5 Individual. On time, substantive, and an open or merged code PR linked = 5; late, thin, or no PR = 3; missing = 0
D8 - Sprint Report 10 Team. Completeness, specificity, quality of evidence; suite health section
D9 - Sprint Release 2 Team. Tag follows convention; created after the last merge; release description summarizes changes
D10 - Reflection Survey 8 Individual. Required for completion
Total 100

D4 - PR grading detail:

The D4 score is the aggregate across all your PRs, normalized to 20 points.

Criterion Points per PR
Change correctly implements the acceptance criteria from D2 6
Tests written or updated appropriately; Test Evidence section complete, with every AC covered and expected values justified 6
PR description explains what changed and why; Tech Debt section present; issue linked 3
CI passes (or manual verification documented) 3
Code reviewed using the rubric (including the test evidence line); reviewer comment posted; PR merged only after an approval on the latest commit 2
Total per PR 20

D6 - Mutation testing rubric:

Criterion Points
Tool run on the files changed by the PR; configuration, command, results, and reports committed 4
Surviving mutants analyzed correctly (equivalent vs. test gap, with explanation) 4
At least one new or strengthened test kills a surviving mutant; re-run confirms it 4
Answers to the questions show understanding, not just description 3
Total 15

CSCI 535: the D6 score is the average of the two submissions.

Minimum bar

A team with no merged PRs (D4), no sprint report (D8), or no release (D9) receives a 0 for Sprint 3 regardless of other deliverables.

Extra credit

A PR submitted to the real upstream project and accepted or under active review earns up to 3 bonus points per PR, at the instructor's discretion.
A bug report filed in the upstream project that comes from your own testing work and is confirmed by the maintainers (by the time Sprint 4 is graded) earns up to 2 bonus points per report, at the instructor's discretion.

// A whole-day entry marks every slot on its date. A partial-day entry marks only the slots that overlap one of
// its windows, so a slot that straddles the leave or return time is away too: a booking there is rejected.
function findOutOfOfficeForSlot(
  dayData: IOutOfOfficeData[string] | undefined,
  windowsOfDay: OutOfOfficeWindowMs[] | undefined,
  slotStartMs: number,

): IOutOfOfficeData[string] | undefined {
  if (!dayData) return undefined;
  if (!windowsOfDay) return dayData;
  return windowsOfDay.find((window) => slotStartMs < window.endMs && slotEndMs > window.startMs)?.data;

function parseOutOfOfficeWindows(datesOutOfOffice: IOutOfOfficeData | undefined) {
  const windowsByDate = new Map<string, OutOfOfficeWindowMs[]>();

  for (const [date, dayData] of Object.entries(datesOutOfOffice)) {

    windowsByDate.set(

      dayData.windows
        .map((window) => ({ startMs: Date.parse(window.start), endMs: Date.parse(window.end), data: window }))
        .sort((a, b) => a.startMs - b.startMs)
    );
  }
  return windowsByDate;
}

337	  return [...slots, ...booked].sort((a, b) => timeOf(a) - timeOf(b));

import { useRouter } from "next/navigation";

import type { IOutOfOfficeData } from "@calcom/features/availability/lib/getUserAvailability";
import ServerTrans from "@calcom/lib/components/ServerTrans";
import { useCompatSearchParams } from "@calcom/lib/hooks/useCompatSearchParams";
import { useLocale } from "@calcom/lib/hooks/useLocale";
import classNames from "@calcom/ui/classNames";
import { Button } from "@calcom/ui/components/button";

interface IOutOfOfficeInSlotsProps {
  date: string;
  fromUser?: IOutOfOfficeData["anyDate"]["fromUser"];
  toUser?: IOutOfOfficeData["anyDate"]["toUser"];
  emoji?: string;
  reason?: string;
  notes?: string | null;
  showNotePublicly?: boolean;
  borderDashed?: boolean;
  className?: string;
}

export const OutOfOfficeInSlots = (props: IOutOfOfficeInSlotsProps) => {
  const { t } = useLocale();
  const {
    fromUser,
    toUser,
    emoji = "🏝️",
    reason,
    borderDashed = true,
    date,
    className,
    notes,
    showNotePublicly,
  } = props;
  const searchParams = useCompatSearchParams();

  const router = useRouter();

  // Check if this is a holiday (no fromUser but has reason)
  const isHoliday = !fromUser && reason;

  // For regular OOO, require fromUser (toUser is optional for redirect)
  // For holidays, we just need the reason
  if (!isHoliday && !fromUser) return null;
  return (
    <div className={classNames("relative h-full pb-5", className)}>
      <div
        className={classNames(
          "flex h-full flex-col items-center justify-start rounded-md border bg-white px-4 py-4 font-normal dark:bg-transparent",
          borderDashed && "border-dashed"
        )}>
        <div className="bg-emphasis flex h-14 w-14 flex-col items-center justify-center rounded-full">
          <span className="m-auto text-center text-lg">{emoji}</span>
        </div>
        <div className="stack-y-2 max-h-[300px] w-full overflow-y-auto text-center">
          {isHoliday ? (
            <>
              <p className="mt-2 text-base font-bold">{reason}</p>
              <p className="text-subtle text-center text-sm">{t("holiday_no_availability")}</p>
            </>
          ) : (
            <>
              <p className="mt-2 text-base font-bold">
                {t("ooo_user_is_ooo", { displayName: fromUser?.displayName })}
              </p>

              {notes && showNotePublicly && (
                <p className="text-subtle mt-2 max-h-[120px] overflow-y-auto break-words px-2 text-center text-sm italic">
                  {notes}
                </p>
              )}

              {fromUser?.displayName && toUser?.displayName && (
                <p className="text-center text-sm">
                  <ServerTrans
                    t={t}
                    i18nKey="ooo_slots_returning"
                    values={{ displayName: toUser.displayName }}
                    components={[<strong key="username">username</strong>]}
                  />
                </p>
              )}
            </>
          )}
        </div>
        {!isHoliday && toUser?.id && (
          <Button
            className="mt-8 max-w-[90%]"
            variant="button"
            color="secondary"
            onClick={() => {
              // grab current dates and query params from URL

              const month = searchParams.get("month");
              const layout = searchParams.get("layout");
              const targetDate = searchParams.get("date") || date;
              // go to the booking page with the selected user and correct search param
              // While being an org push will maintain the org context and just change the user in params
              router.push(
                `/${toUser.username}?${month ? `month=${month}&` : ""}date=${targetDate}${
                  layout ? `&layout=${layout}` : ""
                }`
              );
            }}>
            <span className="block overflow-hidden text-ellipsis whitespace-nowrap">
              {t("ooo_slots_book_with", { displayName: toUser.displayName })}
            </span>
          </Button>
        )}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
};

}));

    isOverlapping: false,
    overlappingTimeStart: "",

    isLocaleReady: true,
    i18n: {},

}));

// The server sends `notes` on an away slot and the panel reads it, but SlotInfo (calendars/lib/types.ts) does not list it.
type Slot = Slots[string][number] & { notes?: string | null };

const host = { fromUser: { id: 1, displayName: "Host" }, emoji: "🩺", showNotePublicly: false };

// 09:00 to 16:00 UTC on 2026-10-08, one slot an hour. The hours listed are away.
const dayWith = (awayHours: number[], awayData: Partial<Slot> = host): Slot[] =>
  Array.from({ length: 8 }, (_, index) => {
    const hour = 9 + index;
    const time = `2026-10-08T${String(hour).padStart(2, "0")}:00:00.000Z`;
    return awayHours.includes(hour) ? { time, away: true, ...awayData } : { time };
  });

const renderDay = (slots: Slot[]) => render(<AvailableTimes slots={slots} event={{ data: null }} />);

// The hours of the slot buttons that come before and after the panel in document order.
const hoursAround = (panel: HTMLElement) => {
  const hourOf = (button: HTMLElement) => Number(button.dataset.time?.slice(11, 13));
  const buttons = screen.getAllByTestId("time");
  return {
    before: buttons
      .filter((button) => button.compareDocumentPosition(panel) & Node.DOCUMENT_POSITION_FOLLOWING)
      .map(hourOf),
    after: buttons
      .filter((button) => button.compareDocumentPosition(panel) & Node.DOCUMENT_POSITION_PRECEDING)
      .map(hourOf),
  };
};

# #130 Away-panel hours: build plan

## Status: waiting for spec review on #130 (no code yet)

The spec is the body of issue #130. This file is the build plan and the draft Test Evidence table, so the PR can open the same day the review lands. Line numbers are from `origin/main` at `247b769fce`.

## Code facts checked on 2026-11-11

- `findOutOfOfficeForSlot` (`packages/features/schedules/lib/slots.ts:16-25`) returns `window.data`, which is the `IOutOfOfficeWindow` with ISO `start` and `end`, but its declared return type is `IOutOfOfficeData[string]`, which has no `start` or `end`. The return type must widen to `IOutOfOfficeData[string] | IOutOfOfficeWindow`, or the new fields cannot be read without a cast.
- The whole-day path returns `dayData` (L23), which has no `start`, so "fields only from a window" (spec note) falls out of a `"start" in data` check.
- Slot data is built at `slots.ts:231-258`. The new fields go in the same spread as `reason` and `emoji`.
- `SlotInfo` (`packages/features/calendars/lib/types.ts:3-12`) has no `notes`. `AvailableTimes.test.tsx:42-43` widens it locally with a comment that says so (criterion 8).
- `AvailableTimes` (`apps/web/modules/bookings/components/AvailableTimes.tsx:274-277`) returns `<OOOSlot {...slots[0]} />` when every slot is away. That is the path criterion 5 changes for two windows.
- The run loop is at L284-307. `isAway(merged[index - 1])` (L301) and `while (isAway(merged[runEnd + 1]))` (L303) join any adjacent away slots. That join is the back-to-back defect.
- `OOOSlot` (L340-369) passes named props to `OutOfOfficeInSlots`, so the two new props must be added to `IOOOSlotProps`, the destructure and the JSX, not only spread.
- `OutOfOfficeInSlots` (`apps/web/modules/bookings/components/OutOfOfficeInSlots.tsx`) prints `ooo_user_is_ooo` (`common.json:3296`). The hours line goes under it, in the non-holiday branch only (criterion 6).
- `useBookerTime()` gives `timeFormat` and `timezone`; `AvailableTimes` already reads both (L272). The test mocks them as `HH:mm` and `UTC` (test L21-23).
- `getPartialDayOutOfOfficeRanges` (`packages/features/schedules/lib/date-ranges.ts:279-284`) has no caller outside `date-ranges.test.ts` (L5, L1297-1370). Removing it (criterion 9) is safe; a grep proves it.
- The existing test "renders one panel per window when a day has two" (test L104) must use two windows with a free slot between them. Check that before relying on it; the new back-to-back test is a separate case.

|---|---|

| `packages/features/calendars/lib/types.ts` | Add `notes`, `windowStart`, `windowEnd` to `SlotInfo` (all optional). |

Adds the date to both times when the two instants fall on different dates in `timeZone`. Uses `@calcom/dayjs`, because the result must follow the booker's time zone. |
| `apps/web/modules/bookings/lib/formatAwayWindow.test.ts` (new) | Criteria 1-3 with no rendering. |

Change the all-away early return so two windows give two panels and one window keeps the whole-day layout plus hours. Pass the formatted hours to `OOOSlot`. |
| `apps/web/modules/bookings/components/AvailableTimes.test.tsx` | Back-to-back, gap shorter than one slot, two windows covering the day, one window covering the day. Drop the local `Slot` widening. |

# Sprint 2 mid-sprint check-in: zach-short

## What did you implement so far in the sprint, and what remains?

As of 2026-10-18, six days into Sprint 2, I have not written Sprint 2 code yet. My work so far is the D1 backlog. I carried my Sprint 1 issue #5 (event theme) into Sprint 2 and re-estimated it from `effort:high` to `effort:medium`, with the scope cut to colors and the image left out. I wrote and posted a new medium issue, #104, which shows the away badge and the redirect for out-of-office entries that cover only part of a day. It picks up a limit I named in my Sprint 1 PR #85. I also created the Sprint 2 milestone and attached both issues to it.

What remains is the build. For #5 and #104 I still need the D2 specs, peer-reviewed before I start coding, and the D3 design decisions with at least two alternatives each. After that come the pull requests with the new Tech Debt section, the AI logs in `ai-logs/sprint2/zach-short/`, and the D6 class and sequence diagrams for one of the two issues.

## What is one thing you learned about the codebase or about software engineering practice?

Code that reads a piece of data can carry assumptions about its shape that the data model does not show. Before PR #85, an out-of-office entry always covered whole days, and the booking page was written around that. `AvailableTimes.tsx` shows the "away" panel only when every slot of a day is away, or when only the first or only the last slot is (lines 266 to 293). `AvailableTimeSlots.tsx` says it outright in a comment, "since OOO is date-level, just check the first slot" (line 206).

PR #85 let an entry carry a leave time and a return time. The `start` and `end` columns were already `DateTime`, so the schema accepted the change without a migration, and the slot engine and its tests were correct. The booker was the part that was not ready: a window in the middle of a day fits neither of its cases. So PR #85 treats a partial-day entry as busy time with no badge, and the badge is now its own issue, #104.

## What is one thing you would do differently?

If I started issue #6 again, I would list every reader of the out-of-office data before I wrote the spec. The entries feed the per-day away map in `getUserAvailability.ts`, the slot builder in `slots.ts`, two booker components, the date picker, the entry list in settings and the API v2 slot output. My spec for #6 named only the schema, the create handler and the form as the parts to change, and it raised the redirect as an open question.

The badge limit came up during the build instead. It went into PR #85 as a known limit, with the alternatives written out in the Design section. By then it was a decision made late, inside a PR that already had 662 changed lines of code. With the readers listed first, the spec could have put the badge out of scope in plain words, or split it into its own issue from the start, and my reviewer would have seen that trade-off before any code existed.

# Sprint 3 mid-sprint check-in: zach-short

**Code PR:** TODO — link the #130 PR here before Nov 12, 11:59 PM (it must be open and ready for review, or merged).

## What have you implemented so far, and what remains?

So far my Sprint 3 work is planning. For the team feature, #131 (OIDC sign-in), I drafted the spec with 43 acceptance criteria, nine design decisions with alternatives, and a breakdown into nine sub-issues with a Sprint 3 demo slice (PR #133). I posted our questions to the customer on #131. For #130 (hours on the partial-day away panel) I wrote the build plan and a draft Test Evidence table, one row per acceptance criterion.

What remains: the #130 code PR after its spec review, my OIDC sub-issue once the team assigns owners, its spec review and PR, and mutation testing with StrykerJS on one of my issues.

## What is one thing you learned about testing in your project?

Passing tests only show that the code does what the tests expect, not what the spec asks. In Sprint 2, PR #125 (waitlist) passed all 45 existing tests, yet a review found three real bugs: a blank panel on fully booked days, a six-hour hold cut to five minutes, and duplicate offers on retry. No test had checked those cases, because the tests followed the code's main path.

So for #130 I wrote the expected values from the acceptance criteria before writing any code. For example, a 14:10 to 14:50 window must print 14:10 and 14:50, not the 14:00 and 15:00 slot times.

## What is one risk to finishing your work by Nov 19, and what will you do about it?

The biggest risk is the OIDC demo. It needs five sub-issues merged in order, and one of them changes the 1,255-line `next-auth-options.ts`, where a mistake in account linking can let one user log in as another. Every sub-issue also needs a spec review and an approval before merge, so a one-day wait at each step adds up.

To reduce this, the breakdown has a merge order so that two people can work in parallel after the first PR. The account-linking code waits for the customer's answer. Until then we reject matching emails, which is safe. I will also ask for reviews on Zulip the day each PR opens.

# Sub-issue 1 (draft): OIDC provider data model and repository

Draft body for the GitHub sub-issue. The owner refines it, posts it as an issue linked to #131, and gets a spec review before code. Criteria numbers in brackets refer to `specs/oidc-sign-in/design.md`. Line numbers are from `origin/main` at `247b769fce`.

**Needs a yes before any edit to `packages/prisma/schema.prisma`** (project rule).

---

### Is your proposal related to a problem?

#131 lets an admin add OIDC providers at run time. Today the only providers are hard-coded and configured with environment variables, and the database has no place to store a provider, its client secret, or its sign-up rules. `IdentityProvider` (`schema.prisma:367`) has no value for an OIDC user. Every other #131 sub-issue (admin backend, admin page, login flow) reads or writes this data, so it comes first.

### Describe the solution you would like

Add an `OIDC` value to `IdentityProvider` and a new `OidcProvider` table with a migration. Add `PrismaOidcProviderRepository`, wired with the moduleLoader DI pattern, that is the only code that reads or writes the table. It returns DTOs, never Prisma types. The client secret is stored only as ciphertext; encrypting it is the admin service's job (sub-issue 3), not the repository's.

### User story

As a developer on the #131 sub-issues, I want one repository for OIDC providers, so that the admin backend and the login flow read the same data in the same way and the secret cannot leak through a query that selects too much.

### User scenario

The admin service (sub-issue 3) calls `create` with an encrypted secret. The login route (sub-issue 5) calls `findEnabled` on each auth request and gets the enabled providers in display order, without their secrets, then calls `findByIdWithEncryptedSecret` for the one provider whose flow it builds. When an admin removes a provider, the service calls `deleteWithAccounts`, and the provider and every user link to it go in one transaction.

### Scope

Medium. It touches the Prisma schema and one migration, a new repository with its DTO, the DI module and container, and unit tests. I expect 6 to 8 files and about 300 changed lines, half of them tests. It adds no UI and no tRPC route.

### Acceptance criteria

1. A migration adds `OIDC` to `IdentityProvider` and creates `OidcProvider` with: `id` (cuid, primary key), `displayName` (text), `issuer` (text), `clientId` (text), `clientSecretEncrypted` (text), `scopes` (text), `allowSignup` (boolean), `allowedDomains` (text array), `enabled` (boolean), `position` (integer), `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `updatedById` (nullable integer).
2. New rows get these defaults: `scopes = "openid email profile"`, `allowSignup = false`, `allowedDomains = []`, `enabled = false`, `position = 0`.
3. Two providers cannot have the same `issuer` and `clientId`. A second insert with the same pair fails with a unique-constraint error, and the repository turns it into an `ErrorWithCode` with a message that names the issuer, not the secret.
4. The migration applies to a database that already has users and accounts, and changes no existing row. `CAL`, `GOOGLE`, `SAML` and `AZUREAD` users keep their values. [39]
5. `findEnabled()` returns only enabled providers, ordered by `position` and then `createdAt`, as `OidcProviderPublicDto` (`id`, `displayName`, `issuer`, `clientId`, `scopes`, `allowSignup`, `allowedDomains`). It never selects `clientSecretEncrypted`. [6, 11]
6. `list()` returns every provider (enabled or not) in the same order and shape as criterion 5, plus `enabled`, `createdAt` and `updatedAt`. It never selects `clientSecretEncrypted`. [6]
7. `findByIdWithEncryptedSecret(id)` is the only method that returns `clientSecretEncrypted`. It returns `null` for an unknown id.
8. `create`, `update` and `setEnabled` write only the fields they are given. `update` without a new secret leaves `clientSecretEncrypted` unchanged. Each returns the shape of criterion 6.
9. `countLinkedAccounts(id)` returns the number of distinct users with an `Account` row whose `provider` is `oidc-<id>`. [36]
10. `deleteWithAccounts(id)` deletes the provider and every `Account` row with `provider = "oidc-<id>"` in one transaction. If either delete fails, neither happens. Deleting an unknown id throws `ErrorWithCode` not-found and deletes nothing. [37]
11. `getOidcProviderRepository()` returns the repository from the DI container, built with `bindModuleToClassOnToken` like `packages/features/credentials/di/CredentialRepository.module.ts`.
12. Every query uses `select`, never `include`. No method returns a Prisma type; the DTOs live in `packages/lib/dto/`.
13. `yarn type-check:ci --force` passes. Code that switches over `IdentityProvider` handles `OIDC` (for example the provider name on `/auth/error`, `apps/web/app/(use-page-wrapper)/auth/error/page.tsx:39-48`, falls back to "your original login method").
14. Unit tests with a mocked Prisma client cover criteria 3 and 5 to 10, including a check that the `select` of `findEnabled` and `list` has no `clientSecretEncrypted` key.

### Out of scope

- Encrypting or decrypting the secret, field validation, the 10-provider limit and the discovery test (sub-issue 3).
- Admin UI (sub-issue 4) and the login flow (sub-issue 5).
- Mapping `oidc-<id>` to `IdentityProvider.OIDC` in `identityProviders.ts` (sub-issue 5).
- Any change to `User` or `Account` columns. The user link is an `Account` row (ADR-002).

### Design decisions

**Where the provider order comes from.** Store an integer `position`, sorted with `createdAt` as the tie-breaker.

1. Sort by `createdAt` only. Rejected: the admin cannot put the main provider first (design criterion 11 asks for an admin-set order).
2. A linked list (`previousId`). Rejected: reordering needs several row updates and is easy to corrupt; 10 rows at most do not need it.

**How `allowedDomains` is stored.** A Postgres text array on the provider row.

1. A separate `OidcProviderDomain` table. Rejected: a second table and a join for at most a handful of strings that are always read with the provider.
2. One comma-separated text column. Rejected: the code must split and trim it everywhere, and a domain with a stray space would not match.

**How a user is linked to a provider.** Use the existing `Account` table with `provider = "oidc-<id>"`, not a new column on `User`. See ADR-002 in `specs/oidc-sign-in/decisions.md`: `Account` already has `@@unique([provider, providerAccountId])` (`schema.prisma:1258`), and a column on `User` would allow only one link per user.

**Who records the last editor.** `updatedById` is a plain nullable integer, not a relation to `User`.

1. A relation to `User`. Rejected: it changes the `User` model, which every Cal.diy query touches, for an audit field nobody joins on.
2. No editor field. Rejected: when two admins edit one provider (design criterion 8), the page cannot say who saved last.

### Technical notes

- Repository pattern: `packages/features/selectedSlots/repositories/PrismaSelectedSlotRepository.ts` (constructor takes `PrismaClient`).
- DI pattern: `packages/features/credentials/di/CredentialRepository.module.ts`; tokens in a new `packages/features/auth/oidc/di/tokens.ts`, spread into `packages/features/di/tokens.ts`.
- Migration folder name: `<timestamp>_add_oidc_provider` in `packages/prisma/migrations/`, after `20261029130000_add_waitlist_entry_slot_start`.
- Run `yarn prisma generate` after the schema change.
- Likely files: `schema.prisma`, the migration, `PrismaOidcProviderRepository.ts` and its test, `packages/lib/dto/OidcProviderDto.ts`, `OidcProviderRepository.module.ts`, `OidcProviderRepository.container.ts`, `tokens.ts` (two files), and `auth/error/page.tsx` if criterion 13 needs it.

### Mutation testing

The repository methods are short and have clear branches (unknown id, unchanged secret, transaction rollback), so StrykerJS can run on `PrismaOidcProviderRepository.ts` with only its own test file.

```

### Peer dependency, Vitest compatibility, and Node engine requirements

Source: https://github.com/stryker-mutator/stryker-js/blob/master/packages/vitest-runner/package.json

The package.json of @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner defines: (1) peerDependencies declares vitest >=2.0.0 as the supported version range, (2) devDependencies pins vitest 4.1.12 for development/testing confirming Vitest 4 compatibility, (3) engines.node >=22.0.0 is the minimum supported Node version.

```json
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=22.0.0"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@stryker-mutator/test-helpers": "workspace:*",
    "@types/node": "24.13.3",
    "@types/semver": "7.8.0",
    "@vitest/browser": "4.1.12",
    "@vitest/browser-playwright": "4.1.12",
    "react": "19.3.1",
    "vite": "8.3.2",
    "vitest": "4.1.12",
    "vitest-browser-react": "2.3.0"
  },
  "peerDependencies": {
    "@stryker-mutator/core": "workspace:*",
    "vitest": ">=2.0.0"
  }
```

--------------------------------

### Vitest Runner > Configuring > vitest.configFile

Source: https://github.com/stryker-mutator/stryker-js/blob/master/docs/vitest-runner.md

### `vitest.configFile` [`string` | `undefined`]

Default: `undefined`

Specify a ['vitest.config.js' file](https://vitest.dev/config/) to be loaded. By default vitest will look for a `vitest.config.js` (or `.ts`) file in the root of your project.

--------------------------------

### Vitest Runner > Configuring > vitest.dir

Source: https://github.com/stryker-mutator/stryker-js/blob/master/docs/vitest-runner.md

### `vitest.dir` [`string` | `undefined`]

_Since v7.1_

Default: `undefined`

Configure the `--dir <path>` command line option. See https://vitest.dev/guide/cli.html#options.

--------------------------------

### Configure vitest runner in stryker.config.json

Source: https://github.com/stryker-mutator/stryker-js/blob/master/docs/vitest-runner.md

Example configuration for the Vitest runner using the stryker.config.json file. Sets testRunner to 'vitest' and provides vitest-specific options like configFile, dir, and related.

```json
{
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "vitest": {
    "configFile": "vitest.config.js",
    "dir": "packages",
    "related": true
  }
}
```

--------------------------------

### Vitest Runner > Configuring

Source: https://github.com/stryker-mutator/stryker-js/blob/master/docs/vitest-runner.md

You can configure the `@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner` using the `stryker.config.json` (or `stryker.config.js`) config file.

```json
{
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "vitest": {
    "configFile": "vitest.config.js",
    "dir": "packages",
    "related": true
  }
}
```
````

import path from "node:path";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { loadEnv } from "vite";
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

const env = loadEnv("", process.cwd(), "");
for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(env)) {
  if (process.env[key] === undefined) {
    process.env[key] = value;
  }
}

const vitestMode = process.env.VITEST_MODE;
// Support both new VITEST_MODE env var and legacy CLI flags for backwards compatibility
// The CLI flags are passed through but Vitest 4.0 doesn't reject them when using yarn test
const isPackagedEmbedMode = vitestMode === "packaged-embed" || process.argv.includes("--packaged-embed-tests-only");
const isIntegrationMode = vitestMode === "integration" || process.argv.includes("--integrationTestsOnly");
const isTimezoneMode = vitestMode === "timezone" || process.argv.includes("--timeZoneDependentTestsOnly");

// Always set INTEGRATION_TEST_MODE to allow server-side imports in jsdom environment
// This is needed because getBookingFields.ts checks for this env var to allow imports
process.env.INTEGRATION_TEST_MODE = "true";

if (isTimezoneMode && !process.env.TZ) {
  throw new Error("TZ environment variable is not set for timezone tests");
}

function getTestInclude() {
  if (isPackagedEmbedMode) {
    return ["packages/embeds/**/packaged/**/*.{test,spec}.{ts,js}"];
  }
  if (isIntegrationMode) {
    return ["packages/**/*.integration-test.ts", "apps/**/*.integration-test.ts"];
  }
  if (isTimezoneMode) {
    return ["packages/**/*.timezone.test.ts", "apps/**/*.timezone.test.ts"];
  }
  // Default: run all test files (Vitest default pattern)
  return ["**/*.{test,spec}.{js,mjs,cjs,ts,mts,cts,jsx,tsx}"];
}

// Set STRYKER_JSON to write the JSON report where the course wants it, for example

/** @type {import("@stryker-mutator/api/core").PartialStrykerOptions} */
export default {
  testRunner: "vitest",
  plugins: ["@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner"],
  vitest: {
    configFile: "vitest.config.mts",
    // Only the tests that import the mutated file run, which keeps a run to minutes in this monorepo.
    related: true,
  },
  // The default sandbox copies the repo and links only the root node_modules, so workspace packages with
  // their own node_modules fail to resolve. Mutating in place avoids that; Stryker restores the files when
  // it exits. Do not edit the mutated files while a run is going, and check `git status` after a crash.
  inPlace: true,
  ignoreStatic: true,
  concurrency: 4,
  timeoutMS: 30000,
  reporters: ["clear-text", "progress", "json", "html"],
  jsonReporter: { fileName: process.env.STRYKER_JSON ?? "reports/mutation/mutation.json" },
  htmlReporter: { fileName: "reports/mutation/mutation.html" },
};

- CI did not run the unit tests at the s2 tag. So I ran 7 suites locally in a separate worktree at the tag. That worktree is now removed.
- Every suite passed, with no failures: schedules 277, auth 100, availability 60, bookings 587, web bookings 64, OOO router 7. The OOO feature folder has no test files.
- Upstream Cal.com authors wrote all the skipped and todo tests. I checked this with `git blame`.
- I found two mistakes in my first draft of this file and fixed them. One claimed a Node 22 result that I had not tested. The other said that the time-zone tests do not run, but they do run.

**3. StrykerJS (D6):** branch `chore/stryker-mutation-setup`
- I added `@stryker-mutator/core` and `@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner` 10.1.1 as root dev dependencies, plus `stryker.config.mjs` and two `.gitignore` lines.
- The command is `TZ=UTC yarn stryker run --mutate <file>`. Set `STRYKER_JSON=docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/<issue>-<user>-before.json` to write the report where the course wants it.
- The test runs passed. `identityProviders.ts` took 7 seconds, with 2 of 2 mutants killed. `AvailableTimes.tsx` took 35 seconds and scored 19.25%. Most of its surviving mutants are in code that #130 does not change.

**Problems that I found and fixed:**
- **In-place mode is not safe here.** In my first run, Vitest read the backup copy, and the restore removed the executable bit from 3 tracked files. I restored those files from git. The config now uses the normal sandbox mode.
- **The sandbox copy failed on symlinks.** It failed on `.claude`, `.cursor` and `packages/prisma/.env`. The config now leaves those paths out of the copy.
- **Node 26:** `yarn prisma generate` exits with code 1, but it still writes every file. Also, `yarn add` failed in the root build step and reformatted a generated file. I restored that file.

To get the Stryker setup to the team, it needs its own PR and a teammate's approval. `yarn.lock` adds about 1,100 lines, but the course does not count lock files toward the PR size.
